scenes.narration: To understand where Abraham Lincoln ended up, start with where Abraham Lincoln began. Abraham Lincoln (February 12, 1809 – April 15, 1865) was the 16th president of the United States, from 1861 until his assassination in 1865. He led the United States through the American Civil War, defeating the Confederacy and playing a major role in the abolition of slavery.

The road from the beginning to the peak of Abraham Lincoln ran through years nobody filmed. Born in a one-room log cabin in Kentucky, Lincoln was raised on the frontier. Angered by the Kansas–Nebraska Act of 1854, which opened the territories to slavery, he became a leader of the new Republican Party.

Each stage of the life of Abraham Lincoln made the next stage possible. His victory prompted a majority of the slave states to begin seceding and form the Confederate States. A month after Lincoln assumed the presidency, Confederate forces attacked Fort Sumter, starting the Civil War.

The people who knew Abraham Lincoln young describe someone already restless. As a moderate Republican, Lincoln had to navigate conflicting political opinions from contentious factions during the war effort. He closely supervised the Union's strategy and tactics, including the selection of generals and the implementation of a naval blockade of Southern ports.

What Abraham Lincoln built in the middle years is what the name still stands for. He suspended the writ of habeas corpus in April 1861, an action that Chief Justice Roger Taney found in Ex parte Merryman that only Congress could do, and he averted war with Britain by defusing the Trent Affair. On January 1, 1863, he issued the Emancipation Proclamation, which declared the slaves in the states "in rebellion" to be free.

By the time Abraham Lincoln reached the defining moment, the preparation was decades old. On November 19, 1863, he delivered the Gettysburg Address, which became one of the most famous speeches in American history. Following his re-election in 1864, he sought to heal the war-torn nation through Reconstruction.

The rise of Abraham Lincoln was not an accident — in retrospect the pattern is plain. On April 14, 1865, five days after the Confederate surrender at Appomattox, Lincoln was fatally shot by John Wilkes Booth at Ford's Theatre in Washington, D.C., becoming the first U.S. president to be assassinated. Lincoln is remembered as a martyr and a national hero for his wartime leadership and for his efforts to preserve the Union and abolish slavery.

Setbacks came early for Abraham Lincoln, and the response to them is the real story. He is consistently ranked in both popular and scholarly polls as among the greatest presidents in American history. Born in a one-room log cabin in Kentucky on February 12, 1809, Abraham Lincoln was raised on Sinking Spring Farm and Knob Creek Farm near Hodgenville, Kentucky.

The legacy of Abraham Lincoln outlived the circumstances that produced it. Nancy is widely assumed to have been the daughter of Lucy Hanks. Thomas and Nancy married on June 12, 1806, and moved to Elizabethtown, Kentucky.

Few lives travel as far as that of Abraham Lincoln, and the distance is the point. Lincoln's father bought multiple farms in Kentucky but could not get clear property titles to any, losing hundreds of acres in legal disputes. In 1816, the family moved to Indiana, where land titles were more reliable.

The childhood of Abraham Lincoln contains the adult in small print. In Kentucky and Indiana, Thomas worked as a farmer, cabinetmaker, and carpenter. At various times, he owned farms, livestock, and town lots, appraised estates, and served on county patrols.

Money, luck and timing all played their parts in the life of Abraham Lincoln — in that order. Thomas and Nancy were members of a Separate Baptist Church, a pious evangelical group whose members largely opposed slavery. Overcoming financial challenges, Thomas obtained clear title to 80 acres (32 ha) in Little Pigeon Creek Community in 1827.

The turning point in the life of Abraham Lincoln looked like a failure at the time. On October 5, 1818, Nancy died from milk sickness, leaving 11-year-old Sarah in charge of the household, which included her father, 9-year-old Abraham, and Nancy's 19-year-old orphan cousin, Dennis Hanks. Thomas married Sarah Bush Johnston, a widow with three children of her own, on December 2, 1819.

Every biography of Abraham Lincoln has to pass through the years that were quietly lost. It included two short stints in Kentucky, where he learned to read, but probably not to write. After moving to Indiana at age seven, he attended school only sporadically, for a total of less than 12 months by age 15.

The education of Abraham Lincoln happened mostly outside any school. Nevertheless, he was an avid reader and maintained a lifelong interest in learning. When Lincoln was a teenager his father relied heavily on him for farmwork and for supplementary income, hiring the boy out to area farmers and pocketing the money, as was the custom at the time.

What Abraham Lincoln wanted at the start and what Abraham Lincoln got are not the same thing, and that gap is the story. In March 1830, fearing another milk-sickness outbreak, several members of the extended Lincoln family, including Abraham, moved west to Illinois and settled in Macon County. Abraham became increasingly distant from Thomas, in part due to his father's lack of interest in education; he would later refuse to attend his father's deathbed or funeral in 1851.

The defining trait of Abraham Lincoln was not talent — it was the refusal to stop. Some historians, such as Michael Burlingame, identify Lincoln's first romantic interest as Ann Rutledge, a young woman also from Kentucky whom he met when he moved to New Salem, Illinois. Lewis Gannett disputes that the evidence supports a romantic relationship between the two.

Those who met Abraham Lincoln at the peak describe someone still running on the early hunger. Lincoln took her death very hard, sinking into a serious depression and contemplating suicide. Late in 1836, Lincoln agreed to marry Owens if she returned to New Salem.

The private years of Abraham Lincoln explain the public decades better than any speech. Owens arrived that November and he courted her, but they both had second thoughts. On August 16, 1837, he wrote Owens a letter saying he would not blame her if she ended the relationship, and she declined to marry him.

The family Abraham Lincoln came from matters more than the legends admit. In 1839, Lincoln met Mary Todd in Springfield, Illinois, and the following year they became engaged. She was a daughter of Robert Smith Todd, a wealthy lawyer and businessman in Lexington, Kentucky.

The first real success of Abraham Lincoln arrived later than anyone expected, and changed everything. Lincoln initially broke off the engagement in early 1841, but the two were reconciled and married on November 4, 1842. In 1844, the couple bought a house in Springfield near his law office.

The last chapter of Abraham Lincoln was written long after the fame. The marriage was turbulent; Mary was verbally abusive and at times physically violent towards her husband. The eldest, Robert Todd Lincoln, was born in 1843, and was the only child to live to maturity.

The whole life of Abraham Lincoln reads like a single decision repeated. Edward Baker "Eddie" Lincoln, born in 1846, died February 1, 1850, probably of tuberculosis. Lincoln's third son, William Wallace "Willie" Lincoln, was born on December 21, 1850, and died of a fever at the White House on February 20, 1862.

Between the birth and the legend of Abraham Lincoln lie the years that actually decide it. The youngest, Thomas "Tad" Lincoln, was born on April 4, 1853, and died of edema at age 18 on July 16, 1871. Lincoln loved children, and the Lincolns were not considered to be strict with their own.

The reputation of Abraham Lincoln was built in the middle, not at the edges. The deaths of Eddie and Willie had profound effects on both parents. Lincoln suffered from "melancholy", a condition now thought to be clinical depression.

Somebody like Abraham Lincoln should not have made it — that is exactly why the story survives. In 1831, Lincoln's father moved the family to a new homestead in Coles County, Illinois, after which Abraham struck out on his own. During 1831 and 1832, Lincoln worked at a general store in New Salem.

The life of Abraham Lincoln begins far from where the story usually starts. He gained a reputation for strength and courage after winning a wrestling match with the leader of a group of ruffians known as the Clary's Grove boys. In 1832, he declared his candidacy for the Illinois House of Representatives, though he interrupted his campaign to serve as a captain in the Illinois Militia during the Black Hawk War.

Abraham Lincoln was not born famous — the early years shaped everything that followed. In his political campaigning, Lincoln advocated for navigational improvements on the Sangamon River. He drew crowds as a raconteur, but he lacked name recognition, powerful friends, and money, and he lost the election.

To understand where Abraham Lincoln ended up, start with where Abraham Lincoln began. When Lincoln returned home from the war, he planned to become a blacksmith but instead purchased a New Salem general store in partnership with William Berry. Because a license was required to sell customers alcoholic beverages, Berry obtained bartending licenses for Lincoln and himself, and in 1833 the Lincoln–Berry General Store became a tavern as well.

The road from the beginning to the peak of Abraham Lincoln ran through years nobody filmed. Burlingame wrote that Berry was "an undisciplined, hard-drinking fellow", and Lincoln "was too soft-hearted to deny anyone credit". Although the economy was booming, the business struggled and went into debt, prompting Lincoln to sell his share.

Each stage of the life of Abraham Lincoln made the next stage possible. Lincoln served as New Salem's postmaster and later as county surveyor, but he continued his voracious reading and decided to become a lawyer. Rather than studying in the office of an established attorney, as was customary, Lincoln read law on his own, borrowing legal texts, including Blackstone's Commentaries and Chitty's Pleadings, from attorney John Todd Stuart.

The people who knew Abraham Lincoln young describe someone already restless. In Lincoln's second state house campaign in 1834, as a supporter of Whig Party leader Henry Clay, he finished second among thirteen candidates running for four places. Lincoln echoed Clay's support for the American Colonization Society, which advocated abolition in conjunction with settling freed slaves in Liberia.

What Abraham Lincoln built in the middle years is what the name still stands for. The Whigs also favored economic modernization in banking, tariffs to fund internal improvements such as railroads, and urbanization. Lincoln served four terms in the Illinois House of Representatives for Sangamon County.
